terroir.climate: Mediterranean with a continental edge: summer days above 35 °C, cool nights because of the altitude and the surrounding ranges, dry winters that can freeze, and rainfall around 400 to 600 millimetres, most of it in autumn and spring storms. The sea is close enough to send humid morning air up the valleys; the Montsant range to the north blocks the colder winds.
terroir.soils: Llicorella: Carboniferous slate and schist, dark brown to black, flaking in thin plates, laced with veins of quartz and almost without organic matter. It drains instantly, reflects heat onto the fruit and forces roots deep into the fractured rock for water. Pockets of clay and granite occur, but slate is the signature the exam wants.
terroir.topography: An amphitheatre of hills between roughly 100 and 750 metres, the vineyards on slopes so steep they are cut into terraces or planted straight up the hillside on costers, the old unterraced pitches. Villages sit at different heights: Gratallops and Bellmunt lower and warmer, Porrera, La Morera de Montsant and Scala Dei higher and cooler, and that difference drives the village wines.
terroir.water: The Siurana river and its tributaries drain the bowl towards the Ebro, and the Siurana reservoir lies to the north east. Water in the vineyard is scarce; vines live on what the slate stores and what their deep roots find.

traps: Priorat is a DOQ, the Catalan spelling of DOCa; Montsant, Penedès and Tarragona are DOs, and Priorat and Rioja alone hold the top rung.
The slate is llicorella: the Douro's schist and the Mosel's slate are cousins, but the exam wants the local word, so name the rock.
Cariñena is the grape (Carignan, Mazuelo, Samsó), and it is also a DO in Aragón; in Priorat the word means the grape.
Vi de Vila is a village tier below Vi de Paratge; the ladder climbs village, site, vineyard, great vineyard, not the other way.
Garnacha, not Tempranillo, is the lead red; Tempranillo is a minor player in Catalonia under the name Ull de Llebre.
Scala Dei is a place and a cellar, not a grape or a wine style; the priory gave the whole region its name.

wines.note: Garnacha and Cariñena, often with Cabernet or Syrah: black cherry, liquorice, graphite and warm stone, high alcohol carried by acidity and firm tannin. Decant young vintages and pour with lamb, game or a rich stew.
A red from one of the twelve named villages, carrying the village on the label; Porrera gives taut Cariñena-led wines, Gratallops riper Garnacha.
Garnacha Blanca, Macabeu and Pedro Ximénez from the slate, sometimes skin-contacted or barrel-aged: pear, fennel, salt and a stony weight. Good with grilled fish and roasted vegetables.
The old fortified and oxidative Garnacha wines of the monks' era, now a tiny production, with a nutty, raisined depth that suits almond pastries and hard cheese.

exam: Name the grape, the climate and the soil in one breath: Albariño, cool wet Atlantic, granite.
Know the five subzones and place Val do Salnés on the coast at Cambados, O Rosal at the Miño's mouth and Condado do Tea upstream.
Know why vines are on pergolas and what the parra is for.
Know the label rule: Rías Baixas Albariño is 100 per cent, the subzone labels 70 per cent.
Hold the Portuguese pairing: Alvarinho, Vinho Verde, Monção e Melgaço.
Be able to say what the wine tastes like and what it is served with: shellfish, cold, young.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: The region's grape by a wide margin: thick-skinned and small-berried, so it stands the damp. Pale, high-acid whites of white peach, citrus, apricot and a saline edge, usually unoaked, sometimes lees-aged for texture or, from old vines, built for a few years in bottle.

grapes.name: Loureira
grapes.styles: Aromatic, floral and lifted, a classic partner for Albariño in O Rosal blends; Loureiro across the border in Portugal.

grapes.name: Treixadura
grapes.styles: Fuller and softer, the companion grape of Condado do Tea blends and the lead grape of Ribeiro further inland.

grapes.name: Caíño Blanco
grapes.styles: A high-acid, late-ripening native used in small measure in Rosal blends for nerve and length.

grapes.name: Godello
grapes.styles: Permitted but a bit-part player here; its home is inland Valdeorras, where it makes broader, stonier whites.

grapes.name: Mencía
grapes.styles: One of several reds allowed, with Caíño Tinto, Espadeiro and Sousón, for the small volume of light, sharp Rías Baixas tinto.

law.classification: Rías Baixas is a Denominación de Origen granted in 1988. An earlier denomination of 1980 was called simply Albariño, which European rules would not allow because a grape name cannot be an appellation, so the DO was re-founded under the name of the coast. The DO is divided into five subzones: Val do Salnés, O Rosal, Condado do Tea, Soutomaior (added in 1996) and Ribeira do Ulla (added in 2000). The label types are set by grape rule: Rías Baixas Albariño is 100 per cent Albariño; Rías Baixas Salnés needs at least 70 per cent Albariño, Rías Baixas Rosal at least 70 per cent of Albariño and Loureira together, Rías Baixas Condado do Tea at least 70 per cent of Albariño and Treixadura together; Rías Baixas on its own needs at least 70 per cent of the preferred varieties. Barrica, Tinto and Espumoso are the further categories.
labels: The grape; on a Rías Baixas label it promises a wine of that grape alone.
On the lees: a wine kept on its fine lees for texture, not a legal term but common on the better labels.
Galician for old vines, used by houses bottling their oldest pergola plots.
A Galician manor house; many bodegas carry the name of the estate they grew from.
Barrel; the DO term for a wine with at least three months in oak.

The single denomination, granted in 1988, covering five subzones in Pontevedra and a corner of A Coruña.

The varietal label: 100 per cent Albariño from anywhere in the DO.

Rías Baixas Salnés, Rosal and Condado do Tea: Salnés at least 70 per cent Albariño; Rosal at least 70 per cent of Albariño with Loureira; Condado do Tea at least 70 per cent of Albariño with Treixadura.

made.viticulture: The pergola, called the parra or emparrado, is the signature: vines trained two metres up on granite posts and wires so that air moves under the canopy and bunches dry quickly after rain, with room to walk, and in the old days to grow cabbages, underneath. It suits a wet climate and Albariño's vigour, though newer plantings on wires with vertical trellising are common where machines can work. Yields are controlled by the DO and the dense old pergola plots are prized. Fungal disease, mildew above all, is the year's running battle, and harvest timing is a bet against the autumn rains: pick early in September and keep the acid, or wait for ripeness and risk rot. Vineyards are small and fragmented, thousands of growers holding plots of under a hectare, many selling to co-operatives or to larger bodegas; this smallholding pattern is why the region was late to bottle and why the co-operative Martín Códax mattered when it formed in the 1980s. Old ungrafted and very old grafted vines survive in Salnés and give the concentrated, long-lived wines a few houses are famous for.
made.winemaking: The default is protective and simple: whole-bunch or destemmed pressing, cold settling, fermentation in stainless steel at low temperature to keep the aromatics, no malolactic as a rule because the acid is the point, a few months on fine lees for texture, then early bottling for release in the spring after harvest. The better houses stretch this: longer lees ageing in tank, bâtonnage, fermentation or ageing in large old oak or foudres, sometimes a touch of malolactic, and bottle age before release, producing wines that are richer, waxier and longer-lived than the fresh norm. The label Rías Baixas Barrica marks a wine that has seen oak for at least three months. Traditional method sparkling is permitted as Rías Baixas Espumoso. The result at the table is a wine that tastes of its weather: high acid, moderate alcohol of 12 to 13 per cent, salt on the finish, and no obvious oak.

places.name: Val do Salnés
places.note: The oldest, largest and coolest subzone, on the flat granite land around the Ría de Arousa in the west of Pontevedra. Its wines are the leanest and most saline, nearly all Albariño, and it holds most of the famous houses and the oldest vines.

places.name: Cambados
places.note: The town that calls itself the capital of Albariño, home of the August Albariño festival since 1953, of the Pazo de Fefiñanes, whose bodega was among the first to bottle the grape, and of the Martín Códax co-operative.

places.name: Meaño and Meis
places.note: Neighbouring Salnés parishes that hold some of the region's most prized old pergolas and the estates of Do Ferreiro and Pazo de Señoráns.

places.name: O Rosal
places.note: The subzone at the mouth of the Miño on the Portuguese border, warmer and sunnier than Salnés, where Albariño is traditionally blended with Loureira and Caíño Blanco for rounder, more floral wines. Terras Gauda is the house most servers meet from here.

places.name: Condado do Tea
places.note: Upstream on the Miño and named for the Tea, a tributary, this is the warmest and most inland subzone, with some slate and schist in its hills. Treixadura is the companion grape and the wines are fuller and softer.

places.name: Soutomaior
places.note: The smallest subzone, added in 1996, at the head of the Ría de Vigo, planted almost entirely to Albariño on granite.

places.name: Ribeira do Ulla
places.note: The last of the five subzones to be added, in 2000, inland along the Ulla river north of Salnés near Padrón, with alluvial soils and a slightly more continental feel; the only part of the DO in the province of A Coruña.

places.name: The Miño and Vinho Verde
places.note: Across the river the grape becomes Alvarinho and the appellation Vinho Verde, with Monção e Melgaço its Alvarinho heartland; the exam likes the pairing and so does a guest comparing the two.

producers.name: Pazo de Señoráns
producers.why: A Salnés estate at Meis whose late-released Selección de Añada showed Albariño could age for a decade.

producers.name: Palacio de Fefiñanes
producers.why: The Cambados palace bodega, founded in 1904, that bottled Albariño under its own name before almost anyone.

producers.name: Martín Códax
producers.why: The Cambados co-operative, founded in 1986 and named for a medieval Galician troubadour, that put Rías Baixas on export lists everywhere.

producers.name: Do Ferreiro
producers.why: A Meaño family house famous for Cepas Vellas, an Albariño from very old pergola vines that rewards bottle age.

producers.name: Terras Gauda
producers.why: The reference O Rosal house, blending Albariño with Caíño Blanco and Loureira.

producers.name: Zárate
producers.why: An old Salnés family bodega at Meaño known for single-plot Albariños and native reds.

producers.name: Pazo das Bruxas
producers.why: The Torres family's Galician Albariño, widely poured by the glass.

terroir.climate: Cool and wet Atlantic maritime. Weather arrives off the ocean, not down from the plateau: mild winters, warm rather than hot summers, and rainfall that can pass 1,600 millimetres in a year, heaviest from autumn to spring and a threat again at harvest. Humidity, not heat, is the grower's enemy, so the whole system of training and harvest is built to keep fruit dry and to pick before the autumn rains. Inland along the Miño the ocean's grip loosens and Condado do Tea runs noticeably warmer than Salnés.
terroir.soils: Granite is the bedrock almost everywhere, weathered into coarse, sandy, free-draining topsoil the Galicians call xabre, mixed with alluvium near the rivers. Condado do Tea adds some schist and slate on its hills. These poor, acidic, quick-draining soils are the counterweight to the rain: water runs through them and the vine is never sodden for long.
terroir.topography: Low and rolling rather than steep: a coast cut by long drowned valleys, the rías, with vineyards on the gentle slopes and valley floors that run down to them, mostly below 300 metres. Val do Salnés is nearly flat around the Ría de Arousa; the Miño subzones climb a little into the hills on the Portuguese border.
terroir.water: The rías themselves, Arousa, Pontevedra and Vigo, flooded river mouths open to the Atlantic, moderate temperature and feed the salt in the air that tasters find in the glass. The Miño forms the border with Portugal; O Rosal sits at its mouth and Condado do Tea upstream, and across the water the same grape is Alvarinho in Vinho Verde's Monção e Melgaço. The Ulla, north of Salnés, gives Ribeira do Ulla its name.

traps: Rías Baixas is in Galicia, the northwest, not the Basque Country; Txakoli is the Basque Atlantic white and a different grape.
Godello and Mencía belong to inland Galicia and Bierzo; Albariño is the Rías Baixas answer.
The subzones are five, not three: Soutomaior and Ribeira do Ulla are easy to forget.
The soil is granite, not slate; slate is Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Priorat.
The DO dates from 1988; the 1980 Albariño denomination was replaced because a grape name cannot be an appellation.
Albariño is not aromatic in the Muscat sense; its lift is peach, citrus and salt, with the acid of a cool climate.

wines.note: Pale straw, bone dry, bright acidity, white peach, lime and a saline finish; serve cold, around 8 to 10 degrees, with oysters, grilled prawns, octopus or ceviche. The region's calling card and the one a server pours most.
The coolest subzone's wine, at least 70 per cent Albariño, leaner and more mineral than the Miño wines; the house style of Cambados and its neighbours.
Blends from the Miño subzones, Albariño with Loureira in Rosal and with Treixadura in Condado, rounder and more floral than Salnés, good with richer fish and chicken.
wines.style: Rías Baixas Rosal and Condado do Tea

wines.note: A growing category: fruit from old pergola vines, long lees contact, sometimes a little oak under the Barrica label, built to hold five years or more and to take on honey and beeswax while keeping its acid.
A rarity: light, sharp, red-fruited wines from Caíño, Espadeiro, Sousón or Mencía, served cool with Galician pork or empanada; useful as a trivia point, rarely on a list.

The climate words: extreme continental, 720 to 1,000 metres, large diurnal range, frost at both ends of the season.
The DO year, 1982, the four provinces with Burgos the largest, and Roa as the Consejo's seat.
Vega Sicilia and Único: founded 1864, Tinto Fino with Cabernet, long ageing; Pesquera and Pingus as the modern and cult landmarks.
The stricter ageing minimums: Crianza 12 months in oak, Gran Reserva 24.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Tinto Fino or Tinta del País locally, a small-berried, thick-skinned plateau clone. Deep purple, blackberry and black cherry, firm tannin, 14 per cent or more, taking French or American oak for Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva; at least 75 per cent of any Ribera red.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The Bordeaux grape Vega Sicilia planted in the 1860s; permitted with Merlot and Malbec in the 95 per cent core of a red, used in small shares for structure and cassis.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: A permitted international blender, softening Tinto Fino in a few estates; rarely more than a seasoning.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Another legacy of the Bordeaux plantings, permitted in the blend and kept in tiny shares.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Garnacha Tinta, limited to a 5 per cent share in reds and used above all for the traditional rosado.

grapes.name: Albillo Mayor
grapes.styles: The native white, once co-planted with Tinto Fino for the old claretes; since the 2020 vintage it may make a white Ribera del Duero on its own or at 75 per cent with other whites.

law.classification: Ribera del Duero was granted its Denominación de Origen in 1982, the first reds of Castilla y León to be recognised; the name was given up by the Peñafiel co-operative founded in 1927, which took the name Protos. The DO spans four provinces, Burgos, Valladolid, Soria and Segovia, with Burgos holding the largest share and the Consejo Regulador seated at Roa. A red must be at least 75 per cent Tempranillo; Tempranillo together with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Malbec must make up at least 95 per cent, with Garnacha Tinta and Albillo Mayor permitted up to 5 per cent. Rosado needs at least half red grapes. White wine was admitted by a rule change approved in March 2020, effective from the 2020 vintage, with Albillo Mayor at a minimum of 75 per cent. Ageing follows Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva with the region's stricter barrel minimums.
labels: The local names for Tempranillo; some labels still carry them.
The native white grape and the base of the new white wine.
Vega Sicilia's blend of several Único vintages, outside the ageing ladder.
The vintage year; on a young wine it is the whole claim.
Vino de la Tierra de Castilla y León
The regional fallback for wine made outside the DO's rules or boundary, used by estates just over the line such as those around Tudela and Sardón.

Granted in 1982; four provinces along the upper Duero; reds at least 75 per cent Tempranillo.
Joven and Roble

At least 24 months of ageing with a minimum of 12 in oak barrel, double the national floor of six.
Reserva
At least 36 months of ageing with a minimum of 12 in oak barrel and the rest in bottle.

At least 60 months of ageing with a minimum of 24 in oak barrel and the rest in bottle; made only in the strong years.
Ribera del Duero Blanco
White wine admitted from the 2020 vintage, at least 75 per cent Albillo Mayor.

made.viticulture: The vineyard is a fight with cold. Spring frost into late May means growers favour slopes over the frost-pooling valley floor, and many still rely on old bush vines, which bud later and sit low, though wire-trained vertical trellising dominates new plantings for machine work. Old vines matter: the region's revival rests on pre-1960s bush-vine Tinto Fino in villages like La Horra, Roa and the Soria uplands around San Esteban de Gormaz and Atauta, where altitude passes 1,000 metres and ripening is slowest. Yields are limited by the DO and the plateau's poverty keeps them low. The season is short: budbreak is late, summer heat is intense, harvest runs from late September into October and an early frost can catch unripe fruit. Diurnal range is the viticultural asset, holding acid in a grape that would lose it on a warmer plain, and the thick skins of the plateau clone give the colour and tannin the wines are known for. Rain is scarce and drought stress in August is common; drip irrigation is permitted under control. Green harvest and leaf removal are routine in the better estates to balance vigour and ripeness.
made.winemaking: Ribera's cellar is darker and more extractive than Rioja's. Long macerations, often three to four weeks, build the deep colour and the tannic frame; fermentation in stainless steel or large wood is followed by malolactic in barrel at the quality end. French oak is far more common than in Rioja, though American barrels are still used, and new wood is a stylistic choice of many houses, giving toast and spice over the blackberry fruit. The ageing categories follow the national ladder, but Ribera's own rules are stricter than the national minimum: Crianza here means at least 12 months in barrel within 24 months of ageing, Reserva at least 12 in barrel within 36 months, Gran Reserva at least 24 in barrel within 60. Vega Sicilia set the older pattern of very long cask ageing, with Único often a decade from harvest to release and a Reserva Especial blended across vintages. The modern wave since the 1980s, led by Pesquera and then Pingus, built the reputation on concentration and ripe fruit; the newer counter-current favours earlier picking, less new oak, concrete and large foudres, and single-village bottlings.

places.name: Burgos stretch
places.note: The heart of the DO by area, with Aranda de Duero the largest town, Roa the seat of the Consejo, and the old-vine villages of La Horra, Sotillo de la Ribera and Gumiel on the high terraces north of the river.

places.name: Roa
places.note: A hilltop town on the Duero and the home of the Consejo Regulador, with limestone slopes and old bush vines around it.

places.name: La Horra
places.note: A village north of Roa famous for very old bush-vine Tinto Fino on sand and clay over limestone; the source of Pingus and of many single-village bottlings.

places.name: Aranda de Duero
places.note: The DO's commercial centre, with medieval wine cellars dug beneath the old town; the Burgos side begins here.

places.name: Valladolid stretch
places.note: The western end around Peñafiel, lower and slightly warmer, and the location of the so-called Milla de Oro, the golden mile of famous estates between Peñafiel and Quintanilla de Onésimo.

places.name: Peñafiel
places.note: The castle town on its ridge, with the Protos cellars beneath and a wine museum within the castle; the symbolic capital of Ribera.

places.name: Pesquera de Duero
places.note: The village where Tinto Pesquera, founded in 1972, began the modern reputation of the region, and where several other leading estates sit.

places.name: Valbuena de Duero
places.note: Home of Vega Sicilia since 1864, Spain's most famous red wine estate; Único and Valbuena 5º carry the village's name across the world, and the sister estate Alión lies a few kilometres upstream towards Peñafiel.

places.name: Quintanilla de Onésimo
places.note: The western limit of the DO and the site of the Pingus cellar; just beyond it Tudela and Sardón de Duero lie outside the boundary.

places.name: Soria stretch
places.note: The high, cold eastern end around San Esteban de Gormaz and Atauta, above 900 metres, with the oldest vines and the latest harvests; a source of fresh, mineral single-village wines.

places.name: Segovia stretch
places.note: A small corner south of the river, the least planted of the four provinces.

producers.name: Vega Sicilia
producers.why: Founded in 1864 at Valbuena; Único, aged around a decade before release, is Spain's most celebrated red and the estate predates the DO by more than a century.

producers.name: Bodegas Alejandro Fernández Tinto Pesquera
producers.why: The Pesquera de Duero house founded in 1972 whose pure Tinto Fino, praised abroad in the 1980s, launched the modern boom.

producers.name: Dominio de Pingus
producers.why: A tiny La Horra old-vine estate whose first vintage, 1995, became Spain's cult red; Flor de Pingus is the second wine.

producers.name: Protos
producers.why: The Peñafiel co-operative founded in 1927 whose original name, Ribera Duero, was given to the denomination.

producers.name: Alión
producers.why: Vega Sicilia's modern sister estate, pure Tinto Fino in new French oak.

producers.name: Aalto
producers.why: A Quintanilla de Arriba estate assembling old-vine fruit from many villages into polished, modern Ribera.

producers.name: Hacienda Monasterio
producers.why: A Pesquera estate on the golden mile known for Tinto Fino with a Bordeaux-trained hand.

terroir.climate: Extreme continental, the harshest of the major Spanish regions. Winters are long and cold, summers hot and dry with little more than 450 millimetres of rain a year, and the altitude drives a diurnal swing that can reach 20 degrees in August. Spring frost is a real hazard into late May and an early autumn frost can end the season in October, so the growing window is short and Tempranillo, an early ripener, is the grape that fits it. The cold nights are the signature: they hold acidity and build colour and tannin in the skins.
terroir.soils: A layered plateau: on the slopes and high terraces, alternating bands of limestone, marl and chalk that the best growers chase for structure and freshness; on the valley floor and the lower terraces, sand and clay with alluvial gravel along the river. Soils vary within a few hundred metres, which is one reason single-village and single-plot bottlings have multiplied.
terroir.topography: The Duero runs west through a broad valley cut into the northern meseta, flanked by flat-topped hills and páramos. Vineyards lie on the valley floor, on the terraces and up to around 1,000 metres on the slopes, higher and colder in Soria at the eastern end than in Valladolid at the western end. The DO stretches roughly 115 kilometres from San Esteban de Gormaz to Quintanilla de Onésimo.
terroir.water: The Duero itself gives the region its name, the riverbank, and the alluvial terraces along it; it flows on west past Rueda and Toro to become Portugal's Douro. Irrigation was once forbidden and remains controlled; the river's main gift is the frost-prone, fog-prone bottomland that the best sites avoid.

traps: Ribera's Crianza needs 12 months in oak, not the national six; candidates quote the national floor.
Tinta de Toro is Toro's Tempranillo; Tinto Fino is Ribera's. Same grape, different valley, and the exam tests the match.
Vega Sicilia is in Valbuena de Duero in Valladolid, not in Burgos, though Burgos holds most of the DO.
The Duero is Ribera's river and becomes the Douro; the Ebro belongs to Rioja.
Abadía Retuerta and Mauro are famous Duero estates but lie outside the DO, under Vino de la Tierra de Castilla y León.
Ribera's white is Albillo Mayor from 2020, not Verdejo; Verdejo is Rueda's grape downstream.
Único is a wine, not a tier; Reserva Especial is a multi-vintage blend, not a legal ageing term.

wines.note: Deep, dark-fruited Tinto Fino with at least a year in oak, firm tannin and vanilla or toast from the barrel; a wine for roast lamb, lechazo, and grilled beef, served around 17 degrees.
Longer-aged wines of structure and savoury depth, leather and tobacco over black fruit; Gran Reserva here is rarer than in Rioja and saved for the strongest years. Decant the young ones.
wines.style: Ribera del Duero Reserva and Gran Reserva

wines.note: Unoaked or briefly oaked reds for the year after harvest, fruit-forward and tannic, the everyday pour of the plateau's bars.
A deep-coloured, full rosé from Tinto Fino and Garnacha, the modern form of the old clarete that was once the region's bread and butter.
The new white from Albillo Mayor, admitted from the 2020 vintage: ripe pear and herbs, often with oak, broad on the palate and low in acid; a curiosity most lists have not yet met.

exam: The ageing ladder with its barrel and bottle minimums, red and white, and the back label colours.
The three zones, their climate and soil, and the 2018 rename of Rioja Baja to Rioja Oriental.
The grapes: Tempranillo, Garnacha, Graciano, Mazuelo and Maturana Tinta; Viura, Malvasía and the 2007 additions.
The dates: DO 1925, Consejo 1926, DOCa 1991, the 2017 reform with Viñedo Singular and sparkling Rioja.
The cask: 225-litre barrica, American oak tradition, the 330-litre cap, the Bordeaux merchants and Haro's station district.
The houses: López de Heredia, CVNE, La Rioja Alta, Muga, Murrieta, Riscal, and the estate movement from Contino onward.
The tasting call: red fruit, vanilla, coconut and dill, soft tannin, and how that differs from Ribera's black fruit and French oak.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: The heart of nearly every red: early-ripening, red-fruited, savoury, with moderate acidity and fine tannin that takes to long oak ageing; strawberry and plum when young, leather, tobacco and dried fruit with cask and bottle age.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Garnacha Tinta adds flesh, warmth and alcohol, and is the traditional grape of Rioja Oriental, though Tempranillo now leads there too; also the base of traditional rosado.

grapes.name: Graciano
grapes.styles: A late-ripening native giving acidity, colour, violets and spice in small shares; prized for Reserva and Gran Reserva blends and bottled alone by a few houses.

grapes.name: Mazuelo
grapes.styles: Rioja's name for Cariñena, or Carignan, bringing tannin and acidity to the blend in modest shares.

grapes.name: Maturana Tinta
grapes.styles: A rare native red recovered from old vineyards and authorised in 2007: deep colour, fresh acidity and a peppery edge in a few modern blends and single variety bottlings.

grapes.name: Viura
grapes.styles: Macabeo, the backbone of white Rioja: neutral and fresh when young, nutty and waxy in the traditional long-oaked whites of Haro.

grapes.name: Malvasía
grapes.styles: Malvasía de Rioja, aromatic and full, the traditional partner of Viura in oaked whites.

grapes.name: Tempranillo Blanco
grapes.styles: A white mutation of Tempranillo found in the 1980s and admitted in 2007, now a fashionable varietal white.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Admitted with Sauvignon Blanc and Verdejo in the 2007 reform, allowed in a white blend but not to lead it.

law.classification: Rioja was the first Spanish Denominación de Origen, recognised in 1925 with a Consejo Regulador from 1926, and in 1991 the first Denominación de Origen Calificada, the top tier of Spanish law. The DOCa covers three zones, Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa and Rioja Oriental, across the provinces of La Rioja, Álava and a corner of Navarra. Five red grapes and nine white are authorised. The ageing terms are legally defined and verified by the numbered back label. A reform approved in 2017 added three claims of origin, Vino de Zona, Vino de Municipio and Viñedo Singular, admitted a traditional method Espumoso de Calidad de Rioja, with Reserva and Gran Añada mentions above the plain category, and in 2018 renamed Rioja Baja as Rioja Oriental. Wine outside the rules falls to the regional category, not to Rioja.
labels: The 225-litre barrel; the law caps ageing casks at 330 litres.
A grower's young wine, usually carbonic maceration, drunk the year after harvest.
The Consejo's numbered back label whose colour states the tier.
Cariñena, or Carignan, in the Rioja blend.
The eastern zone, Rioja Baja until 2018.
The vintage tier of sparkling Rioja, 36 months on lees.
tiers: DOCa Rioja
The denomination itself: DO in 1925, DOCa in 1991, the first in Spain on both counts.
Genérico, young
A wine with no required ageing; green back label marked Garantía de Origen; the Alavesa cosechero reds sit here.
Crianza
Red: at least 24 months of ageing with 12 in barrel; white and rosado: at least 18 months with 6 in barrel. Red back label.
Reserva
Red: at least 36 months with 12 in barrel and 6 in bottle; white and rosado: 24 months with 6 in barrel. Burgundy back label.
Gran Reserva

Red: at least 60 months with 24 in barrel and 24 in bottle; white and rosado: 48 months with 6 in barrel. Blue back label; by custom made only in strong vintages, though the law fixes only the ageing.
Vino de Zona
A wine from one of the three zones, named on the label, under the 2017 reform.
Vino de Municipio
A village wine from one named municipality, the middle rung of the 2017 origin claims.
Viñedo Singular
A named single vineyard of minimum age, hand harvested at reduced yields and passed by a tasting panel; the top origin claim, from the 2017 vintage.
Espumoso de Calidad de Rioja

made.viticulture: The traditional vineyard is a low bush vine, en vaso, planted at moderate density on terraces and small plots, and bush vines still cover much of Alavesa and the older Alta; new plantings are wire-trained for machines on the flatter Oriental land. Tempranillo buds and ripens early, which suits a valley where the season is cut short by autumn rain in the west and by heat in the east, and harvest runs from late September in Oriental into October under the sierra. Spring frost and hail are the hazards of the high western terraces; drought is the east's. Garnacha goes where it is hot and Graciano where there is time to ripen it. The Consejo sets yield limits and a cask rule, and its back label stamps every bottle. Old-vine plots, hand harvest and a minimum vine age underpin the Viñedo Singular category of 2017, which rewards a named vineyard rather than a blend across the valley. The smallholding pattern persists: thousands of growers sell to the large houses and the co-operatives, and a grower's own cosechero red, made by whole-bunch carbonic maceration in an open stone lago, is the Alavesa village tradition.
made.winemaking: The cask made Rioja. Bordeaux merchants who came to the Ebro when oidium and then phylloxera ruined their own vineyards in the 1850s to 1880s brought the 225-litre barrica, and the houses that gathered around Haro's railway station from the late 1870s, drawn by the railway that had reached the town in 1863, kept it, choosing American oak for cost and for the coconut, vanilla and dill it lends; long cask ageing, racking by hand every six months, and release only when the wine was ready became the house style, and whites were treated the same way. The modern style from the 1970s onward picked riper, extracted more, used French oak and new barrels, and bottled sooner, and most houses now sit between the two. The law fixes the ladder: casks of 330 litres or less; red Crianza at least 12 months in barrel within 24 of ageing; Reserva at least 12 in barrel and 6 in bottle within 36; Gran Reserva at least 24 in barrel and 24 in bottle within 60; whites and rosados six months in barrel for all three, within 18, 24 and 48 months. Carbonic maceration gives Alavesa's young reds; blending across zones and grapes remains the signature of the great houses, and the Consejo's coloured back labels, green for a young wine, red for Crianza, burgundy for Reserva and blue for Gran Reserva, tell a server the tier from across the room.

places.name: Rioja Alta
places.note: The western and highest part of the south bank, plus the Sonsierra on the north bank within La Rioja: cooler, Atlantic-tinged, calcareous and ferrous clay, home of the classic long-aged houses and most of the famous names.

places.name: Haro
places.note: The wine capital of the west, whose Barrio de la Estación, the station district where bodegas gathered beside the railway, open since 1863, from the late 1870s, holds López de Heredia, CVNE, La Rioja Alta, Muga, Gómez Cruzado, Bodegas Bilbaínas and Roda within a few hundred metres.

places.name: Logroño
places.note: The regional capital on the Ebro and the seat of the Consejo Regulador; Marqués de Murrieta's Ygay estate lies on its edge, where Alta meets Oriental.

places.name: Cenicero and Fuenmayor
places.note: Mid-valley towns of large bodegas between Haro and Logroño, on terraces of clay and gravel.

places.name: San Vicente de la Sonsierra and Briones
places.note: San Vicente and neighbouring Ábalos form the Sonsierra, the north-bank corner of La Rioja beneath the sierra, with some of the oldest bush vines and a cluster of single-vineyard producers; Briones faces them across the Ebro from the south bank.

places.name: Rioja Alavesa
places.note: The north bank in Basque Álava, terraced calcareous clay rising towards the Sierra de Cantabria, the smallest zone: pure Tempranillo, old bush vines on small plots, carbonic cosechero reds and, from the 1970s, the modern single-estate movement.

places.name: Laguardia
places.note: The walled hill town at the centre of Alavesa with wine cellars under every street; the base of Artadi, which withdrew from the DOCa in 2015 over the lack of vineyard terms.

places.name: Elciego
places.note: Home of Marqués de Riscal, founded in 1858, which with Murrieta, the first of the two, brought Bordeaux methods to the valley in the mid nineteenth century; its modern winery building is a landmark.

places.name: Labastida and Laserna
places.note: Labastida holds Remelluri, a single estate in the foothills; Laserna, near Oyón, is the site of Contino, a single-vineyard estate since 1973.

places.name: Rioja Oriental
places.note: The eastern zone, Rioja Baja until 2018, lower and hotter on alluvial and ferrous clay plains, with Garnacha its traditional grape and much of the volume; parts of it lie in Navarra.

places.name: Alfaro
places.note: The easternmost wine town, the base of Palacios Remondo and the modern case for old-vine Garnacha from the Oriental hills.

places.name: Calahorra and Aldeanueva de Ebro
places.note: Towns of the hot Ebro plain where co-operatives and large bodegas make the fruit-driven, Garnacha-rich reds of the zone.

producers.name: R. López de Heredia Viña Tondonia
producers.why: Haro's time capsule, founded in 1877: Viña Tondonia and its siblings are aged for years in old American oak and released when mature, whites included.

producers.name: CVNE (Compañía Vinícola del Norte de España)
producers.why: Founded in Haro in 1879; Imperial and Viña Real are the textbook Reserva and Gran Reserva of the classic style.

producers.name: La Rioja Alta S.A.
producers.why: A Haro house of 1890 whose Gran Reserva 904 and 890 define traditional long-aged Rioja.

producers.name: Bodegas Muga
producers.why: Haro's station-district house with its own cooperage, bridging the traditional and modern styles.

producers.name: Marqués de Murrieta
producers.why: The Ygay estate at Logroño, making wine since 1852, the first of the two houses, with Riscal, to bring Bordeaux methods to Rioja; Castillo Ygay Gran Reserva Especial comes from its own vines.

producers.name: Marqués de Riscal
producers.why: Elciego, founded in 1858: with Murrieta, whose winemaking began in 1852, one of the two houses that brought Bordeaux methods to Rioja in the mid nineteenth century, and later the maker of modern Rueda.

producers.name: La Granja Nuestra Señora de Remelluri
producers.why: A Labastida single estate in the Alavesa foothills, an early sign of the estate movement.

producers.name: Viñedos del Contino
producers.why: A single vineyard at Laserna bottled on its own since 1973, the first estate wine of modern Rioja.

producers.name: Artadi
producers.why: Laguardia's single-vineyard pioneer, with Viña El Pisón, which left the DOCa in 2015 to argue for vineyard labelling.

producers.name: Bodegas Palacios Remondo
producers.why: The Alfaro house that made old-vine Garnacha from Rioja Oriental respectable again.

producers.name: Roda
producers.why: A Haro house of 1987 and a flagship of the modern, French-oak, single-estate approach.

terroir.climate: Three climates in one valley. The west, Rioja Alta and Alavesa, is continental with an Atlantic touch: cooler, wetter at around 450 to 500 millimetres, with the Sierra de Cantabria to the north shielding the vines from the storms of the Bay of Biscay an hour away. The east, Rioja Oriental, is lower, hotter and drier, Mediterranean in feel, with Garnacha the grape that suits it. Altitude runs from about 700 metres in the Alavesa foothills down to 300 metres at Alfaro, and the span is why a Rioja blend from several zones was the historic norm.
terroir.soils: Rioja Alta carries calcareous clay on its higher terraces, ferrous clay in reddish patches and alluvial gravel beside the rivers; Rioja Alavesa is almost all calcareous clay on terraces beneath the sierra, pale and chalky, with small walled plots; Rioja Oriental is alluvial and ferrous clay on the valley floor. Calcareous clay is the soil the finest Tempranillo prefers.
terroir.topography: A broad valley about 100 kilometres long and 40 wide, walled by the Sierra de Cantabria and the Obarenes to the north and the Sierra de la Demanda to the south, descending eastward with the Ebro. Alavesa's vineyards sit on sloping terraces under the limestone wall; Alta's on terraces and hills south of the river; Oriental's on open plains where the valley widens towards Navarra.
terroir.water: The Ebro, Spain's great Mediterranean-bound river, is the valley's axis, and seven tributaries from the Demanda, the Oja, Najerilla, Iregua, Leza, Cidacos and Alhama among them, cut the south bank into the ridges where the Alta's best sites lie; the Oja is one candidate for the region's name. The river's fog in autumn is a hazard on the lowest land.

traps: Gran Reserva is five years with two in barrel and two in bottle under the current rules; the older teaching of three years in bottle is out of date, though the five-year total stands.
Reserva is three years with one in barrel and, under the current rules, six months in bottle; Crianza is two years with one in barrel. Do not swap Reserva's and Gran Reserva's barrel minimums.
Rioja Baja no longer exists on labels; it is Rioja Oriental, since 2018.
Mazuelo is Carignan, not Mourvèdre; Graciano is a native, not a synonym of anything.
Rioja Alavesa is in the Basque Country, Álava, not in the region of La Rioja; the DOCa crosses three political regions.
White Rioja may contain Chardonnay or Sauvignon Blanc but Viura and the natives must lead; the 2007 reform widened the list without changing the character.
Viñedo Singular is a labelling claim for a named vineyard, not an ageing term, and it sits beside Crianza or Reserva rather than replacing them.

wines.note: Young, unoaked or barely oaked Tempranillo, often made by carbonic maceration in Rioja Alavesa; bright, grapey, drunk cool with tapas within a year or two.
At least a year in barrel and two in all: red fruit with vanilla and spice from the oak, soft and ready; the everyday bottle for roast chicken, chorizo or lamb chops.
Three years of ageing with at least one in oak and six months in bottle: fuller, more savoury, leather and dried cherry; the classic pairing for roast lamb, served at 17 to 18 degrees.

Five years at least, two in barrel and two in bottle, by custom made only in strong vintages (the law fixes only the ageing) and often released a decade or more after harvest: mellow, complex, coconut and tobacco from American oak in the traditional houses; an old, traditionally made Gran Reserva often throws a deposit and is decanted off it.

From Viura with Malvasía, either fresh and neutral or, in the old Haro style, aged for years in oak into a nutty, oxidative white with something of old Sherry about it that goes with rich fish and cured meats; modern Tempranillo Blanco sits between.

Garnacha-based rosé, at least a quarter red grapes, and since 2017 a traditional method sparkling Rioja: at least 15 months on lees for the plain category, with the mentions Reserva and Gran Añada above it.

exam: Rueda is Verdejo, Toro is Tinta de Toro: grape, colour and province, Valladolid and Zamora.
The dates: Rueda 1980, the first DO of Castilla y León; Toro 1987.
The label percentages: Rueda Verdejo 85, Rueda Sauvignon 85, plain Rueda 50; Toro reds 75 per cent Tinta de Toro.
Why Rueda picks at night and why Toro still has ungrafted vines: oxidation in the one, sand in the other.
Marqués de Riscal's 1972 move as the origin of modern Rueda; Numanthia and Pintia as modern Toro.
How Verdejo tastes against Sauvignon Blanc: fennel, bay leaf and bitter almond rather than gooseberry.
Gran Vino de Rueda as the 2021 old-vine quality mark.

grapes.name: Verdejo
grapes.styles: Rueda's grape: aromatic, herbal and citrus, with fennel, bay leaf and a bitter almond finish, oily in texture, apt to oxidise, so it is picked at night and made cold; lees-aged and barrel-fermented versions age well.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Planted in Rueda from the 1970s and allowed its own varietal label at 85 per cent; grassier and sharper than Verdejo, and often blended with it.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Tinta de Toro in Toro, a thick-skinned, small-berried form grown as old bush vines, making black-fruited, tannic reds of 14 to 15 per cent that take new oak; at least three quarters of a Toro red.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Toro's permitted red partner and the base of its rosado; a minor player in a Tinta de Toro world.

grapes.name: Viura
grapes.styles: Macabeo, a neutral white permitted in the basic Rueda blend, which needs only half Verdejo.

grapes.name: Palomino
grapes.styles: The Sherry grape, once the base of Rueda's flor-aged Dorado and Pálido, now a shrinking share of the vineyard.

law.classification: Rueda was recognised as a Denominación de Origen in 1980, the first in Castilla y León, across Valladolid, Segovia and Ávila. Its labels are grape rules: Rueda Verdejo needs at least 85 per cent Verdejo, Rueda Sauvignon at least 85 per cent Sauvignon Blanc, and plain Rueda at least 50 per cent Verdejo with Viura, Palomino and the other permitted whites. Rueda Espumoso is traditional method sparkling, and Dorado and Pálido are the historic aged styles. Red and rosé wines were admitted under the DO in 2008. Gran Vino de Rueda, launched in 2021, is a quality mark for wines from vineyards over 30 years old at reduced yields, passed by a tasting panel. Toro became a DO in 1987 in Zamora; its reds must be at least 75 per cent Tinta de Toro, with Garnacha the permitted partner, and alcohol may not exceed 15 per cent. Both use the national ageing terms.
labels: Rueda's grape; on a Rueda Verdejo label it is at least 85 per cent.
On the lees, a common claim on fuller Verdejo.
Pre-phylloxera vines, a claim seen on old-vine Toro and the sands of Nieva.
tiers: DO Rueda
Granted in 1980, Castilla y León's first; a white wine denomination at heart, with reds and rosés admitted in 2008.
Rueda Verdejo
At least 85 per cent Verdejo; the label most guests will know.

At least 85 per cent Sauvignon Blanc.
Rueda
At least 50 per cent Verdejo, the balance from the other permitted whites.
Gran Vino de Rueda
A quality mark launched in 2021 for wines from vineyards over 30 years old at a maximum of 6,500 kilograms per hectare, approved by a tasting panel.
Rueda Dorado and Pálido
The historic aged wines: Dorado oxidative in oak and golden, Pálido aged under flor.
DO Toro
Granted in 1987 in Zamora; reds at least 75 per cent Tinta de Toro, alcohol capped at 15 per cent, national ageing terms.

made.viticulture: Rueda's growers harvest at night, by machine, because Verdejo browns and loses its aromatics with heat and air; cool fruit arrives at the press in the dark and is protected from the start. Most of the modern vineyard is on wires for that machine, but old bush vines, including ungrafted plots on the sands of Nieva, give the concentrated wines the Gran Vino de Rueda rules reward, with their minimum vine age of 30 years and yield cap of 6,500 kilograms per hectare. Spring frost and summer drought are the hazards; irrigation is used under control. Toro's vineyard is older in character: low bush vines, widely spaced on sand and pebbles, many on their own roots from before phylloxera, yielding tiny crops of thick-skinned Tinta de Toro that ripen fast in the heat. The grower's problem in Toro is not ripeness but restraint, picking before sugar runs away and tannin turns coarse; the DO caps alcohol at 15 per cent. Both regions are dry, windy and bright, and both have seen heavy investment from outside since the 1990s.
made.winemaking: Rueda's cellar is reductive and cold: gentle pressing, often with a short skin contact for aromatics, cold settling, fermentation in stainless steel at low temperature with selected yeasts, no malolactic, a spell on lees and early bottling, which is why the typical wine is fresh, grassy and ready in the spring. The serious houses ferment old-vine fruit in barrel or foudre and age it on lees for a year or more, following the lead set in the 1990s by Belondrade. The historic Dorado and Pálido survive as curiosities, aged in cask oxidatively or under flor. Toro's cellar is about managing power: careful extraction from thick skins, malolactic in barrel, and ageing in French and American oak under the national Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva terms, with new oak used generously by the modern houses. The best Toro is tamed by old vines and a lighter hand; the plainest is simply big.

places.name: Rueda
places.note: The white-wine DO south of Valladolid on the stony plateau, with the towns of Rueda, La Seca, Serrada and Nava del Rey at its core and Medina del Campo, the old fair town, at its southern edge.

places.name: La Seca
places.note: The village with the densest concentration of bodegas and the old Verdejo plots on cascajo; the working capital of the DO.

places.name: Medina del Campo
places.note: The market town whose medieval fairs made Rueda's golden Dorado famous across Castile centuries before Verdejo was fermented cold.

places.name: Nieva
places.note: A Segovia enclave at the DO's eastern edge where sandy soils kept Verdejo bush vines ungrafted through phylloxera; the source of the region's oldest-vine wines.

places.name: Toro
places.note: The red-wine DO around the town of Toro in Zamora, west of Rueda and downstream on the Duero, on sand and pebbles over clay; Tinta de Toro bush vines, some on their own roots, make its dense reds.

places.name: Toro
places.note: The walled hill town above the Duero that names the DO, with cellars dug under its streets and the Consejo in the town.

places.name: San Román de Hornija and Villafranca de Duero
places.note: Villages on the Valladolid side of the DO holding some of the oldest vineyards, with the Pintia estate at San Román de Hornija.

places.name: Valdefinjas and Morales de Toro
places.note: Villages south and east of Toro where Numanthia and several modern houses farm old bush vines.

producers.name: Marqués de Riscal
producers.why: The Rioja house that came to Rueda in 1972 with a Bordeaux consultant and launched modern cold-fermented Verdejo.

producers.name: Belondrade
producers.why: The La Seca estate that showed, from 1994, that barrel-fermented, lees-aged Verdejo could age like white Burgundy.

producers.name: Ossian
producers.why: Old ungrafted Verdejo on the sands of Nieva, the oldest-vine expression of the grape.

producers.name: Palacio de Bornos
producers.why: A large Rueda house, widely poured, that helped carry Verdejo onto lists abroad.

producers.name: Numanthia
producers.why: The Toro estate founded in 1998 whose old-vine Tinta de Toro brought the region cult prices.

producers.name: Pintia
producers.why: Vega Sicilia's Toro project at San Román de Hornija, a polished, cellar-driven take on Tinta de Toro.

producers.name: Teso La Monja
producers.why: A Toro estate known for very old ungrafted bush vines and dense single-plot reds.

producers.name: Fariña
producers.why: The pioneer family bodega of the Toro DO whose Colegiata label kept the name alive before the boom.

terroir.climate: Both are continental and dry. Rueda, at 700 to 800 metres, has cold winters, hot summers with cool nights, around 400 to 500 millimetres of rain and a frost risk in spring; the night-time chill is what keeps Verdejo's acidity. Toro, lower at roughly 600 to 750 metres and further from the mountains, is hotter and drier still, with long hot summers that push Tinta de Toro to 14 or 15 per cent alcohol, moderated only by cold nights and a short autumn.
terroir.soils: Rueda's signature is cascajo, a bed of rounded stones and gravel over clay and limestone on the high terraces, with pure sand around Nieva in Segovia where ungrafted pre-phylloxera Verdejo survives. Toro's are sandy and pebbly over clay, with some limestone, poor and well drained; the sand is why phylloxera could not spread and why bush vines of great age still stand on their own roots.
terroir.topography: A broad, flat, high plateau either side of the Duero, open to wind and sun with little relief. Rueda spreads south of the river around the towns of Rueda, La Seca and Medina del Campo; Toro sits on terraces along the river and the gentle slopes around the town of Toro, with the land falling slowly westward towards Portugal.
terroir.water: The Duero runs through both, past Tordesillas and the town of Toro, on its way from Ribera to the Portuguese border where it becomes the Douro. The river marks Rueda's northern edge and cuts Toro in two, but neither region leans on it for climate; the sea is far away and the plateau is dry.

traps: Verdejo is not Verdelho; the Madeira grape is unrelated.
Tinta de Toro is Tempranillo; Tinto Fino is the Ribera name. Match the synonym to the valley.
Rueda is in Valladolid, Toro in Zamora; both are Castilla y León, neither is Rioja or Galicia.
Rueda Dorado is oxidative and Pálido is flor-aged; swapping them is a classic slip.
Rueda Verdejo needs 85 per cent, plain Rueda only 50; the grape name on the label is the clue.
Toro's alcohol is capped at 15 per cent, high but legal; it is not a fortified wine.

wines.note: Pale, dry, aromatic: grapefruit, fennel, cut grass and a bitter almond twist, medium body and brisk acid; served cold with seafood, asparagus, goat's cheese or a green salad, and the Spanish answer to Sauvignon Blanc by the glass.
The varietal Sauvignon Blanc of the plateau, greener and sharper than Verdejo, at least 85 per cent of the grape.
Fuller wines from old vines, lees and oak, waxy and nutty with age; the Gran Vino de Rueda category launched in 2021 marks the best of them from vines over 30 years old.
The historic styles: Dorado aged oxidatively in oak to a golden, nutty, Sherry-like wine, Pálido aged under flor; rarities that explain why Palomino is still planted here.
Opaque, black-fruited Tinta de Toro with heavy tannin, ripe alcohol and often new oak; Crianza and Reserva versions are built for roast meats and game, and want air and a few years.
A deep, fruity rosé from Garnacha and Tinta de Toro, the local summer pour.

exam: The pyramid, top down: DOCa/DOQ (Rioja and Priorat only), Vino de Pago, DO, Vino de Calidad, Vino de la Tierra, Vino.
The national ageing minimums and the two regions that tighten them, Rioja and Ribera del Duero.
Tempranillo's synonyms by region, and Garnacha, Monastrell and Cariñena under their French names.
Rioja and Jerez in depth; Ribera, Priorat, Rías Baixas, Rueda and Cava in outline.
The rivers: Ebro for Rioja and Navarra, Duero for Ribera, Rueda and Toro, Miño and Sil for Galicia and Bierzo.
The dates that anchor the story: Rioja DO 1925 and DOCa 1991, Ribera 1982, Priorat DOQ 2009, the 2003 law.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: The national red: Rioja's silk, Ribera's muscle, Toro's weight, La Mancha's volume, with a local name in almost every region.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Spanish by origin, most likely from Aragón: the flesh of Rioja Oriental and Navarra, the heart of Priorat with Cariñena, the base of rosado.

grapes.name: Mourvèdre / Monastrell
grapes.styles: The hot-country red of Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante: dark, ripe, tannic, often from old ungrafted bush vines.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Cariñena, Mazuelo or Samsó: acid and tannin for Rioja blends and a lead grape of old-vine Priorat.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.styles: The Atlantic white of Rías Baixas, saline and peachy.

grapes.name: Verdejo
grapes.styles: Rueda's herbal, bitter-almond white, picked at night and fermented cold.

grapes.name: Palomino
grapes.styles: The Sherry grape, neutral on its own, transformed by flor and the solera.

grapes.name: Airén
grapes.styles: The most widely planted white in Spain, the neutral bulk grape of La Mancha's plain, much of it distilled for brandy.

grapes.name: Macabeo
grapes.styles: Viura in Rioja: the main white there and one of Cava's three grapes with Xarel·lo and Parellada.

grapes.name: Mencía
grapes.styles: The fragrant red of Bierzo and Galicia's slate valleys.

grapes.name: Godello
grapes.styles: The textured white of Valdeorras and Bierzo.

grapes.name: Pedro Ximénez
grapes.styles: Sun-dried for the sweetest Sherry and the wines of Montilla-Moriles.

Oak: a brief spell in barrel below Crianza, a term used by producers rather than fixed in national law.

spain.overview:
Vines came with the Phoenicians and the Romans, survived the Moorish centuries, and Jerez shipped wine to the north of Europe from the Middle Ages on. The modern story begins in the nineteenth century, when oidium and then phylloxera drove Bordeaux merchants south to the Ebro, bringing the 225-litre barrica and the habit of ageing wine in it; Rioja's first DO in 1925 and the ageing terms grew from that cask. Phylloxera arrived late, around 1900 in Rioja, and sand kept a few old vineyards in Toro, Rueda and Jumilla on their own roots. The long middle of the twentieth century belonged to co-operatives and bulk wine, and the revolution came from the 1970s: Pesquera and then Pingus in Ribera, the Priorat pioneers on their slate, cold-fermented Verdejo in Rueda, Albariño bottled in Galicia, the single-estate movement in Rioja and the rescue of old-vine Garnacha and Monastrell everywhere.

The geography is a high plateau, the meseta, ringed by mountains and sloped to the Atlantic in the west: Galicia and the Basque coast are green and wet, the Duero and Ebro valleys continental, Catalonia and the Levante Mediterranean, Andalucía hot and bright. Altitude is Spain's hidden cool climate, and most of the serious reds grow above 500 metres. The Duero leaves for Portugal as the Douro; the Ebro, Rioja's river, is the one great stream that reaches the Mediterranean. Jerez sits on the Atlantic coast near Cádiz on white albariza chalk, and Cava is made across four zones with Penedès at its heart.

The law of 2003, the Ley de la Viña y del Vino, set the pyramid now carried under the European scheme of protected origins: at the top, Denominación de Origen Calificada, DOQ in Catalan, held by Rioja since 1991 and Priorat since its Catalan grant of 2000 and national confirmation of 2009; then the Denominaciones de Origen, which are the working tier; Vino de Pago for a single estate with its own appellation, Dominio de Valdepusa the first in 2003; Vino de Calidad con Indicación Geográfica as a stepping stone; Vino de la Tierra as the IGP country wine; and plain Vino. The ageing terms are national minimums that regions may tighten: a red Crianza is 24 months with 6 in oak, a Reserva 36 with 12, a Gran Reserva 60 with 18; whites and rosados take 18, 24 and 48 months with 6 in oak at every step. Rioja and Ribera del Duero ask for 12 months in barrel for Crianza and 24 for Gran Reserva.

The exam leans on Rioja and Jerez hardest, then Ribera del Duero and Priorat, then the grapes and their synonyms: Tempranillo as Tinto Fino, Tinta de Toro, Cencibel and Ull de Llebre; Garnacha as Grenache; Monastrell as Mourvèdre; Mazuelo and Cariñena as Carignan; Viura as Macabeo. Know the two DOCa regions, the ageing minimums, Cava's three grapes and traditional method, the Sherry styles and the albariza, and the Atlantic white of Rías Baixas, and the Certified paper will hold few surprises.

traps: Reserve means law in Spain and nothing in France or the United States; Reserva's barrel minimum is twelve months, Gran Reserva's eighteen nationally and twenty-four in Rioja and Ribera.
Only Rioja and Priorat hold the top tier; Ribera del Duero, Jerez and Cava are DOs.
Cava is a DO defined by method and grapes, not by one town; Penedès is its historic centre, not its boundary.
Tempranillo changes name but not identity: Tinto Fino, Tinta de Toro, Cencibel and Ull de Llebre are the same grape, Tinta Roriz across the Portuguese border.
Garnacha is Grenache and Spanish by origin; Monastrell is Mourvèdre; Mazuelo is Carignan. Mencía is none of these.
Vino de Pago is a single estate's own appellation, not a tier above DOCa in prestige by law; it sits beside the DOs.
Jerez wines are fortified and the ageing is a solera, so Crianza and Reserva do not apply there.
